en: Preface to the Elucidation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* In my observation of those who have annotated this sūtra, they all tend toward lofty discourse on the ultimate and the subtle, displaying their rhetorical prowess while disregarding the sequence of the preceding and following passages of the text.
Consequently, their interpretations often contradict one another; at times, the pursuit of profundity only serves to increase obscurity. If one hopes that...

Those who uphold, recite, and explain it to others are few. At this time, while my mind was beset by distress and my thoughts were in turmoil, I have privately borrowed several sections and unraveled them.
I have selected those explanations that are clear and manifest and recorded them.

Regarding the divisions of the sūtra and the location of its underlying intent, I have ventured—not out of confidence in my own meager learning—to supplement them with my humble views, all based upon the sūtra itself.

Whether explained horizontally or vertically, reiterated and repeated, there is nothing that does not take the clarification of mind and the realization of nature as the essential core of the Gate of Non-duality.
Without resorting to ornate rhetoric, this may be explained by anyone; perhaps it will be of some small benefit. Some say:

"If the Buddha intended to show people the clarification of mind and the realization of nature, he would have simply spoken the Dharma directly. Why, then, did he speak according to [the capacities of beings] throughout the sutras?"
[The interlocutor] followed the sweeping and seemed as though he wished to seek the origin in its subtle details. I said, "No, no. This is precisely where one perceives the compassion of the Buddha.
Why is this? Because the nature of the human mind is fundamentally luminous; it is only because it has become submerged in the four marks and the six sense objects [that it appears otherwise]."
Because they have lost their original luminosity, the Buddha was compelled to resort to provisional verbal explanations.

If a person can restore that original luminosity, then all verbal teachings and metaphors become mere superfluous additions. If one does not sweep these away, it is a manifest case of claiming the Buddha-dharma for oneself—a state the Buddha did not intend.
This is because he wished for people to contemplate within the very midst of speech and thereby return [to the source].
He immediately swept the area and contemplated it; suddenly, he awakened to his original nature. It was for this reason that the Buddha spoke out of necessity.
This is precisely the profound intent behind the Tathāgata’s protective mindfulness and entrustment.
Preface to the Donated Publication of the *Kongjiejing Chanshuo* (An Exposition on the Diamond Sūtra), inscribed by Cunu, a man of the White Clouds from ancient Min,
at Jingxin Hall in Huayuan, Suzhou, during the first ten days of the seventh month in the autumn of the twenty-first year of the Jiaqing era.
It is heard that the Way of the Buddha is vast and profound; it benefits all beings through its compassion. Its divine efficacy is immense; it awakens humanity through its wisdom.
Thus, it existed before heaven and earth, yet its beginning is unseen; it will exist after heaven and earth, yet its end is unseen. Contemplating the Golden [Light]...
The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra may indeed be seen as such. This sūtra discusses the emptiness that is not empty and realizes the marklessness of marks.
It elucidates the nature of delusion, which can be understood through the six aspects of existence; it investigates the fundamental source, which can be awakened to within the four marks.
Truly, it is the profound essence of the Buddhas’ transmission of the lamp and the central lineage for expounding the Way of the Mahāyāna. And...

It is the mind-dharma by which all sentient beings clarify the mind and perceive its nature. Although the Dharma is attained through the mind, there is no means to embody this Dharma except through the sutras.

The sutras are elucidated by people, yet there is no means to manifest the sutras except through words. The world transmits the sutras, yet there is no means to make them public to the world except through carving them into woodblocks.
From the Tang and Song dynasties down to the Yuan and Ming, those who have commented upon this sutra and carved it into print have been numerous.
The various schools and lineages have proliferated until books fill the halls and exhaust the oxen that carry them;

yet, in seeking one who has analyzed the ultimate correctness of the true words and reconciled the secret intent without deviation, none is more detailed than the *Kongōkyō* exposition of the Mountain Man of White Clouds.
As for this Mountain Man of White Clouds, he was the late Mr. Chen Cunwu, a former provincial graduate from the ancient region of Min. His courtesy name was Yu.

Chapter. His person served in the administration of a flower-county, where he tested the harmony of stringed music and song; his official duties spanned the Yellow Hall, where he nurtured the blossoms of spring.
In his leisure from public affairs, he looked up with admiration toward True Suchness (Tathatā) and expounded upon this sutra.

He thoroughly elucidated the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), such that those who read it would be like gazing upon a precious mirror in the midst of heaven, and those who recite it would be as if finding a bright pearl in the vast blue sea. Alas, it is a pity that due to the seeds planted by his mind...
The fruit—pears and jujubes—has not yet reached maturity; this is indeed fortunate. To take merit as one’s field, one’s descendants shall guard it forever.
Yet, for every single character and every scroll, one must rely on the power of the donor (*dānapati*); every inch of paper and every inch of woodblock is none other than the patron’s gold.

Thus, we hope that those who delight in goodness will share the same heart, and we look toward those who enjoy giving so that no trace of stinginess remains. Whether they generously contribute white coins, it truly belongs to...
Magnificent and grand in its natural ease. Should you wish to assist with the "qingfu" (copper coins), I pray that the more there are, the better.

I humbly entreat you all to witness this heart as true as a sunflower and lend your voices, however briefly, like lotus petals, so that these words may be engraved upon scrolls and spread abroad to broaden the compassion of the Tathāgata, and distributed for circulation to fully awaken the wisdom of all sentient beings. This serves as the preface.

Preface to the General Rules, respectfully composed by Hong Shouchun of Taiyang during the summer of the year Dingmao (the sixth year of the Tongzhi era) at the Western Pavilion of the Xunle Shanfang in Haedong.
The authentic principles annotated in this scripture have all been collated, annotated, and excerpted by the Governor Deng Kuīyuán.

I have followed the original text without recording the names of those who provided the annotations. As for other passages where the views of certain masters were adopted, I have recorded their names;
it was not out of a desire to seize credit for myself.
This sutra has traditionally been divided into thirty-two sections, each with its own title, falsely attributed to the arrangement of Prince Zhaoming of the Liang dynasty;
this appears to be a shallow and superficial approach. It is likely that later generations also divided it into several chapters, yet even these have not proven to be entirely satisfactory.
For now, I shall proceed by explaining it directly section by section. May the reader...
One can naturally realize the ultimate destination through this.
There are many points of divergence among the various editions of this sutra, such as the reasons for [certain phenomena] and the explanations of their names, and so forth.
Whether present or absent, [these marks] are all unimpeded in their textual meaning; however, we shall now follow the original edition.

In this sutra, a single circle is used at essential points, double circles are added at particularly crucial points, and a single slash is used at the conclusion of major sections, so that readers may have clear vision.
The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Ancient Min. Compiled by Baiyun Shanren Cunku (Cunwu Shi).
Expounded by his great-grandson, Zifu Houji Chen Shi. Collated and published.
"Gold" refers to iron. It is produced from within gold; even after being refined a hundred times, it does not diminish. It is the most firm and sharp, capable of severing and destroying all things.
It is like wisdom (*prajñā*), which can sever and eliminate greed, anger, delusion, and all inverted views. This is *prajñā*.
In the language of China, *prajñā* is translated as "wisdom. *Pāramitā* is translated as "reaching the other shore.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of the six *pāramitās*: first, *dāna-pāramitā*, which is giving; second, *śīla-pāramitā*, which is observing the precepts;
third, *kṣānti-pāramitā*, which is patience; fourth, *vīrya-pāramitā*, which is diligence; fifth, *dhyāna-pāramitā*...
"Honey" refers to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). The six *prajñāpāramitās* refer to wisdom. These six are also known as the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
"Sūtra" is the Sanskrit term for *sūtra*.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yaoqin [Dynasty].
Yaoqin was a small state during the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Eastern Jin. Previously, Fu Jian was the King of Qin; his son Pi succeeded him as emperor, establishing the Fu Qin.
After the eleventh year of the Taiyuan era, the King of Qin, Yao Chang, declared himself emperor. (The nineteenth year...)
In the year [of] Chang, he passed away. Crown Prince Xing ascended the throne; this was the Yao Qin dynasty. Regarding the Tripiṭaka Master:

it is said that one who is versed in the three collections of Dharma—the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras—of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna is a teacher of the great assembly. His name in Sanskrit is Kumārajīva;

in the language of China, it means "Child-Longevity," signifying that although he was a youth, he possessed the virtues of the aged. He was originally a person from India, [and later went to] Kucha in the Western Regions.
This man was the nephew of the King. At the age of seven, he entered the monastic order; he recited a thousand verses daily and immediately mastered their meaning.
Emperor Yao Xing of the Qin dynasty invited him into the Xiaoyao Garden to translate various scriptures. As the teachings entered China, the texts were all in Sanskrit;
having obtained successive generations of Western monks who were proficient in the Chinese language, they translated the Sanskrit texts into Chinese characters for the benefit of the Middle Kingdom.
People recite this sutra, which was translated by Kumārajīva:
"Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī... [until] having washed his feet, he spread out a seat and sat down."
In the Sanskrit language, *buddha*; in the language of China, "the Awakened One" (*jùzhě*). The one who preached this sutra was Śākyamuni Buddha.
In the Sanskrit language, *Śākyamuni*; in the language of China, "Capable Benevolence and Silent Stillness. His clan was Kṣatriya; his father was King Śuddhodana.
His mother was Māyā. On the eighth day of the fourth month in the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, the year of Jiayin, he was born from the right side of Māyā’s flank.
He left the household life at the age of nineteen and attained enlightenment at the age of thirty.
He entered *nirvāṇa* on the fifteenth day of the second month in the fifty-second year of King Mu of the Zhou dynasty, the year of Renshen. One thousand one hundred years after his passing...
In the seventeenth year [of the Buddha’s ministry], the teaching reached the Central Xia (China); this was precisely the tenth year of the Yongping era of the Later Han, the *wuchen* year.
Thus, speaking of the entire canon as a whole: the word “I” (*aham*) is a self-designation used by Ānanda, the Buddha’s younger brother.

In Sanskrit he is called Ānanda; in Chinese, it means “Joyous Celebration. He was the youngest son of King Śuddhodana—or, according to some accounts, his nephew. On the day the Buddha attained enlightenment...

He was born, and the entire nation celebrated with joy; thus he was named [Ānanda]. At the age of twenty, he left the household life. Another ten years passed, and the Buddha appointed him as his attendant (*upasthāyaka*).
When the Buddha was about to enter *parinirvāṇa*, Ānanda inquired regarding the essential purport of all the sūtras and what words should be placed at the beginning.

The Buddha said: "One should place: 'Thus have I heard' (*evam mayā śrutam*); at one time, the Buddha was at such-and-such a place, together with such-and-such persons. This was to ensure that for all generations throughout the world...
World-Honored One, you know that the Dharma has its source and origin; it is not something that worldly people can speak of recklessly.
Śrāvastī is the kingdom of King Prasenajit in Central India. The Prince’s name was Jeta, and because this grove was bestowed by Jeta, it is called Jetavana.
As for the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden, there was a minister of the king named Sudatta who constantly...
In this country, he provided relief to the solitary and the poor; thus people called him the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The Elder Sudatta was originally a native of Śrāvastī. Initially, he did not know the Buddha. For the sake of seeking a bride, he entered the city of Rājagṛha from Śrāvastī.
Through Saṃthaṇa, he saw the Buddha and conceived faith, inviting him to return to Śrāvastī. The Buddha then commanded him..."

The Prince selected a location for his residence and found the Jeta Grove. When the Elder asked for its price, the Prince replied in jest, "If you can cover the ground with gold, then it shall be sold.
The Elder spread the gold, and the Prince was moved to admiration; he then exchanged the site with him.
All the trees on the land were also given to the Buddha, and thus a vihāra was established. Both the Elder and the Prince gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.

Therefore, it is called the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. “Bhikṣu” is translated in the language of China as “mendicant” (qǐshì). He begs for food to sustain his body and begs for the Dharma to sustain his mind.
The term “great bhikṣu” (dàbǐqiū) is used to indicate that he has mastered the Mahāyāna. The Buddha is the Honored One of the three realms.

Therefore, he is called the World-Honored One. Regarding his begging for food: although the Buddha was a prince of the Golden Wheel-turning Kings, he personally carried his alms bowl to beg for food in order to teach and transform sentient beings, thereby relinquishing pride and arrogance.
At that time, the Elder Subhūti—[the passage continues with] "how should one dwell, and how should one subdue the mind.
The Elder is renowned for his seniority and virtue; Subhūti is the Chinese translation of "Excellent Appearance" (*Śobhita*), though it is also interpreted as "Excellent Speech."
One tradition says his name was Kūṭadanta (Empty-born). On the day of his birth, the entire household became empty. His parents were startled and amazed;

a physiognomist divined that it was both auspicious and favorable, and thus he was named accordingly. He was one of the great disciples of the Buddha. [Recorded in] Changshui’s *Jing-sbu* (Commentary on the Sūtra).

"Exposed shoulder" (*tàn*) refers to baring the upper body. It is a secular custom of the Western Regions that upon seeing a king, one must bare the upper body to show that one does not dare to commit any offense.
Buddhism also adopts this practice accordingly; however, here it serves to signify that one is about to shoulder the heavy burden of great virtue.

Baring one shoulder, kneeling with the knees touching the ground, and joining the palms—all these are the rites of that country. Respectfully regarded, they constitute the gateway for entering the Way.
One should respect all things; how much more so when wishing to receive and hear the holy teachings? "Tathāgata" is a title of the Buddha.
It is called "Tathā" (Thus) because his clarity illuminates immeasurable worlds without obstruction, and his wisdom penetrates the events of immeasurable eons without hindrance;
he is able to manifest in all manner of forms for the sake of all sentient beings without limit.
It is not so. This is truly that which accords with the self-as-it-is (*tathatā*). It is called "coming" because the true nature manifests according to conditions as it arrives.

If a person offers prayers with utmost sincerity, there is a corresponding response; if one wishes to establish transformation for all sentient beings, the form-body (*rūpakāya*) manifests—all these are instances of its "coming.
"As" (*ru*) refers to the fundamental essence of the true nature; "coming" (*lai*) refers to...

This is the application of the true nature (*tathatā*). "Guarding and mindful entrustment" means that the Tathāgata gives rise to a heart of compassion (*karuṇā*) to protect and cherish [beings], so that they may believe and accept this Dharma; he commits and entrusts them so that they may practice this Dharma.
At the beginning of the assembly’s hearing of the Dharma, Subhūti had no other concern than his sole wish that the Tathāgata give rise to a heart of compassion.

This refers to being protected by mindfulness and entrusted [with the teachings]. "Bodhisattva" is a general term for one who cultivates the Way. In Sanskrit, it is *bodhisattva*, which is an abbreviated form.
*Bodhi* translates into Chinese as "the path of awakening" (*jùdào*); *sattva* translates into Chinese as "a sentient being of great resolve" (*dàxīn zhòngshēng*).
Because they enter the Buddha-way with a great mind, they are called Bodhisattvas. "All Bodhisattvas" refers here to the entire assembly.
*A* is glossed as "non-"; *anuttara*, as "supreme"; *samyak*, as "correct"; *sambheda*, as "equal"; and *bodhi*, as "awakening."
Regarding the term "Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment" (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*): it is vast and all-encompassing, with nothing further to be added; hence it is called "unsurpassed.

It is equally possessed by both the spiritual and the sentient, being impartial regardless of high or low status; hence it is called "perfectly equal" (*samyak*). All principles are fully perfected within it, and its perfect luminosity shines everywhere;
hence it is called "perfect enlightenment" (*saṃbodhi*). "What should one dwell upon? means: what should one contemplate while dwelling? "How should one subdue... [the mind?]
"Subduing the mind" means: how should one subdue this mind of deluded thoughts? Sengruo Ne said:
Subhūti has precisely raised these two questions; first, he asks about sentient beings who resolve upon the unsurpassed mind and seek prajñā.
How does one abide in the principle of the Truths? How does one subdue the mind of afflictions? How does one suppress and gather back the distracted mind?
What is taught in the sūtras does not go beyond these states of abiding and subduing.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti" (up to) "...yes indeed, World-Honored One, I wish and desire to hear.
"Excellent" praises the urgency of his question. "Attentively examine" means to scrutinize with care. "Thus" refers to what is stated in the following text.
"Yes" is a prompt response. "Indeed" is an affirmation of those words. "I wish and desire to hear" refers to Subhūti.
The joy [of the Buddha] was so profound that he did not even notice the redundancy of his words.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "A bodhisattva-mahāsattva... [up to] ...one who possesses the mark of a self is not a bodhisattva."
This section explains the subduing of the mind. The reason "subduing" is mentioned first and "abiding" later is like saying one must first eliminate private desires before preserving principle.
However, when it says "abiding" through "subduing," the latter is already contained within the former. *Mahā* is the Chinese translation for "great."
Those born from eggs comprise the class of fish, birds, tortoises, and snakes. Those born from wombs comprise the class of humans, domestic animals, nāgas, and sages.
Those born from moisture comprise the class of wriggling and crawling insects. Those born by transformation comprise the class of metamorphic beings and flying creatures. These are those with form.

Those who are refined and clear regarding auspicious and inauspicious signs belong to one category; they are formless. Those who are dispersed, dissolved, or submerged in emptiness belong to another category; they possess perception.

Those who are spirits, ghosts, or numinous intelligences belong to another category; they lack perception. Those whose spirit and consciousness have transformed into earth, wood, metal, or stone belong to another category.

"Neither with perception nor without perception" refers generally to those *pudgalas* mentioned in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* who, failing to understand the wondrously enlightened mind of clarity, have delusively followed the seven destinies and become immersed therein; this refers to their *nirvāṇa*.
In the language of China, this is called "perfect stillness" (yuánjì). It is the nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), which is what the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* refers to as "Great Nirvana.
It is that upon which all practitioners rely and take refuge. Master Zongmi’s *Commentary and Sub-commentary* states: "Non-arising is 'nir' (nirodha), and non-extinction is 'vāṇa' (vāna).
This is perfect purity, wherein subject and object are entirely extinguished; it is the transcendence of saṃsāra and the departure from birth and death. That is to say:
To mistake reaching the ultimate state of the other shore for death is a great error. There are four types of *nirvāṇa*:

first, *svabhāva-nirvāṇa* (intrinsic nirvāṇa), which is shared by both ordinary beings and sages; second, *apratisthita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding nirvāṇa), which pertains to the response-transformations of all Buddhas;

third, *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder), where those of the small vehicle have only severed the views and afflictions of the triple world but have not yet escaped ignorance; and fourth, *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder).
Nirvana means already being liberated and exhausted; therefore, it is called "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*). "Extinction" refers to the total extinction of ignorance and afflictions.

"Crossing over" refers to crossing over and being liberated from the ocean of birth-and-death suffering. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: "The fundamental nature of all sentient beings is eternally extinguished."
There is no further extinction. The *Platform Sutra* of the Sixth Patriarch Huineng says: "To deliver oneself by means of one's own nature is called true deliverance.
When Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked the World-Honored One, "If in reality there are no sentient beings who attain extinction (nirvāṇa), how is this so?
The World-Honored One replied: "Nature is fundamentally pure; it is without birth and without extinction. Therefore, there are no sentient beings who attain extinction, nor is there nirvāṇa."

One may reach this state; all of these are attributed to sentient beings, yet the Buddha does not claim them as his own merit. Regarding "marks" (*lakṣaṇa*), these refer to outward traces. The Sixth Patriarch said: "Practitioners also have four marks.
To have a sense of self-sufficiency and to look down upon other sentient beings is called the mark of self (*ātman*).

To rely on one's own observance of the precepts and to look down upon those who break them is called the mark of person (*pudgala*). To loathe the sufferings of the three miserable realms and to wish to be reborn [in heaven]..."
O devas, these are the marks of a sentient being: the mind cherishes long life and diligently cultivates meritorious deeds, clinging to dharmas without forgetting them;
this is the mark of a self. Where there are these four marks, one is a sentient being; where there are no four marks, one is a Buddha.
Furthermore, Subhūti, regarding the bodhisattva’s [practice] toward the dharmas... the bodhisattva should simply abide as instructed.
Furthermore, this refers to the Buddha’s repeated and sequential responses to Subhūti’s questions. This section explains abiding in the mind;
however, the explanation of abiding while descending [into non-abiding] is already contained therein. "To have no abode" means that the mind does not grasp.
[The Buddha] said: "Subhūti, regarding the question of abiding in the mind, the Buddha teaches that non-abiding is itself abiding.

'Generosity' refers to the practice of giving by means of the Dharma for the liberation of sentient beings. The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind constitute the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

Form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena constitute the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). The character 'contact' (*chù*) encompasses a broad range; it includes everything with which the body must engage."
This is so. "Dharma" (fa) is like the colloquial term for "method"; it refers to whatever is planned by the mind. "Merit" (fu) is the application of virtue; "virtue" (de) is the root of merit.
The six sense faculties of ordinary people are impure; they crave the six objects of the senses to satisfy their desires.
If one does not obtain what they desire, they will inevitably practice giving in order to fulfill that desire;
this is the case for those who give while remaining attached to something. A bodhisattva, however, receives the knowledge of the Tathāgata’s teaching on signlessness and has no seeking after desires.
There is no thought of being able to give; one benefits sentient beings solely through the gift of Dharma. It is like water moving through the earth, meeting with no obstruction;
such is the case for one who practices giving without dwelling anywhere. "No, World-Honored One.
Having thus answered, Subhūti again addresses the Buddha, calling him by his title as a mark of respect and intimacy; subsequent instances follow this pattern. Xie Lingyun said:
The words of the Sage are without error; the principle cannot be transgressed. One should simply settle the mind according to the Buddha’s teaching.
To abide as taught is precisely what the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* means by "abiding through the dharma of non-abiding.
These three preceding sections encompass the general purport of the entire scripture; hereafter, the specific items will be discussed in detail, investigating them layer by layer.
[This is] the aggregate (*skandha*).
Subhūti, what do you think? (up to: "The so-called mark of the body is not a mark of the body.
The mark of the body is the physical body (*rūpakāya*); to see the Tathāgata means to see the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The Buddha told Subhūti: "Whatever has marks... [until] if one sees that all marks are no-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.
"Whatever has marks is entirely false and illusory"—these four lines are the most essential words in the sutra;
they are called the "Four-Line Stanza" (*catuṣpāda-gāthā*), which refers to the passage cited below. Regarding the two preceding sections, Subhūti has attained realization concerning bodily marks.
It is not a sign, yet the Buddha immediately expands upon this to instruct him: "To see the Tathāgata" means to see the Tathāgata within one's own mind.
This is like clouds and mist clearing away so that the blue sky appears; when desire is purified, the heavenly principle remains.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One... (down to) 'even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas.

This passage represents the Buddha’s compassionate heart in exhorting students; it is his protective mindfulness (*anuparigṛhīta*). Throughout the entire scripture, he exercises this protective mindfulness, which is here made explicit.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The great ocean of the Buddha-dharma can be entered through faith alone. This is indeed the case.
"Faith" is the stairway to the ultimate truth. "Pure" means unmixed. Master Ruona said: "The characteristic of dharmas is having views;
the non-characteristic of dharmas is being without views. Because one abandons attachment to these two extremes, it is called 'non-existent.
That which the mind pursues is called 'grasping'; grasping leads to attachment. For this reason, one does not dwell upon characteristics."

This is the meaning [of the teaching]. As for the analogy of the raft: a raft is a structure of woven bamboo used to cross water; it serves as a metaphor for how a person may rely upon the Buddha-dharma to reach the other shore.
Master Fu said: "To cross the river, one must use a raft; once the shore is reached, the boat is no longer needed.
These words fully express the point.
"Subhūti, what do you think... [up to] ...all have their distinctions based on the dharma of non-action (asaṃskṛta-dharma)?

Subhūti replied: "It is not a dharma, therefore it does not exist; it is not a non-dharma, therefore it is not non-existent. That both existence and non-existence are absent is the ultimate principle.
This accords with the statement that there is no mark of dharmas (dharmanimitta) and also no mark of non-dharmas. O Worthy One.
Bodhisattvas, Arhats, and the assembly of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are all noble ones; that is to say, they are Buddhas.
As for "unconditioned dharmas" (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), they accord with the spontaneity of true nature and involve no deliberate activity.

Subhūti knew that attaining unconditioned dharmas is truly the profound depth of awakening to the Way. It is like performing good deeds in order to obtain merit, while refraining from evil out of fear.
That one meets with calamity is always due to having acted. One should simply act according to principle: it is right to do good and wrong to do evil.

Even if doing good brings calamity, it must certainly be done; even if doing evil brings fortune, it must certainly not be done. It is merely a matter of acting with a steadfast mind. To have distinction is the mark of the worthy (*bhadra*);
thus there is the Samādhi of Non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*). To be a sage (*ārya*) is to abide in suchness (*tathatā*).
"It is movement.
Subhūti, what do you think? ... Therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.
These two preceding sections represent the point at which Subhūti attained realization. In the Buddhist scriptures, this is situated beyond this world.

Chen Zizifu is my most intimate friend. He once said to me: "In the past, our late ancestor, Lord Cunwu, served as the Prefect of Changzhou.
In his leisure time between official duties, he composed a vast amount of works that must surely be worth viewing. It is a pity that they have not reached you, sir."
Separated by north and south, we were unable to share the examination of these traces of your ancestors' handling—a source of regret. I said: "These are the writings of your late grandfather.
Having brought them back from eight thousand *li* away, you have cherished them for over fifty years.

Among them, those that pertain to the principles of name and teaching (*mingjiao*) and may be transmitted to future generations ought to be promptly entrusted to the carver's tool (*jige*) to be made public to the world; only then will they not fail to serve their purpose."
This great event of continuing and transmitting [the legacy] is not merely for the sake of viewing, reading, or aesthetic appreciation. Luofu responded, saying, "Indeed, indeed.
By the time of the Renxu year of the Tongzhi era, the region was embroiled in turmoil, and Luofu’s family was besieged. Two or three months passed.
Once the siege was lifted, the perilous situation turned into safety. People said that from within the house there emerged the hand of a giant, as large as a chariot wheel;
the crowd dispersed in terror. Later, when Luo Fu searched throughout the room, he found no other objects at all, except for a single book chest left by his ancestors upon a stand.
Upon opening it to read, he found they were all official documents; he took up the scrolls one by one to examine them, and they fluttered away like drifting clouds.
As for the compilation, it was only through the single volume explaining the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* that I finally realized this hand; is this seal perhaps that of Vajrapāṇi?
This volume was also what I had habitually recited with devotion. Unexpectedly, several dozen characters have been stolen by bookworms.
Thereupon, Ji-zufu was moved by my previous words; he transcribed the text and presented it to me, requesting that I [complete it].
I supplemented it. He said, "My previous words were merely in jest. Is this matter actually true now? However, such matters are indeed not things our school should discuss;
therefore, I did not dare record them previously. That I have specifically recorded them here at the end is because I have failed to measure my own ignorance and simplicity.
Now, having read his writings thoroughly and examined his arguments closely, I have humbly extracted their essence to...
Upon completing this supplement, I have come to realize that our late Master’s dedication was arduous and his enduring legacy profound.

Thus, in elucidating this scripture, he did no more than draw upon the text to hear its meaning and rely on that meaning to compose his exegesis; yet his intent was thoroughly penetrating, making it easy for people to attain awakening.
It is clear that he possessed the true spirit of a Confucian patriarch, being fundamentally different from those who engage in lofty talk of the mysterious and the sublime.

I therefore joyfully propose that we together assist in this endeavor. It is my hope that the compassionate heart behind the exposition of these teachings will not go unappreciated, and it shall suffice as proof that virtuous people have their successors.
Thus, one may call this "inconceivable merit," or one may call it "inconceivable karmic retribution"—either is perfectly appropriate.
